newsitem.title: FRANCE: Foccart dead, French Africa policy in turmoil.
newsitem.headline: Foccart dead, French Africa policy in turmoil.

text.p: The death of veteran Gaullist Africa kingmaker Jacques Foccart on Wednesday highlighted disarray in France's African policy under President Jacques Chirac, a self-proclaimed "Afro-optimist".
Foccart, an honorary adviser to Chirac, symbolised an era when France made and broke governments in West and Central Africa on the basis of its political and commercial interests.

Diplomats said the shadowy former spymaster, who ensured France continued to pull the strings after decolonisation, ran one of two parallel and often contradictory Africa policies right up to the last few days.

From an office in the Elysee presidential palace, Foccart continued to support ageing pro-French autocrats while Chirac's official policymakers sought to promote democratic and economic reforms in former French colonies.

Ironically, Foccart died as one of France's longest-standing proteges, ailing Zaire strongman Mobutu Sese Seko, faces the most severe challenge to his 32-year rule from rebels backed by African governments allied with the United States.

"We see today in Zaire that French policy is being beaten into retreat by the Americans," said his biographer, Pierre Pean. "I believe there is a symbol in the fall of Kisangani, the impending fall of Mobutu and the death of Jacques Foccart.
"It is indeed the end of an era, of a certain French Africa policy," he said.
Until recently, the newspaper Le Monde reported, Foccart was responsible for Chirac's contacts with Mobutu.
Other proteges still in power include Gnassingbe Eyadema in Togo, Omar Bongo in Gabon and Paul Biya in Cameroun.

Foccart's death comes at a time of waning French influence in Central Africa, due to Tutsi victories in Rwanda and Zaire, although Paris still holds considerable sway in West Africa and is seeking closer ties with oil-rich, English-speaking Nigeria.

Diplomats say a shift towards a more modern Africa policy, rewarding political and economic pluralism and the rule of law and emphasising investment rather than aid handouts, is likely to be gradual, with exceptions for old friends of France.
"France has several Africa policies and there is still a gap between the rhetoric (on good governance) and the reality," one Paris-based Africa watcher said.
In many African countries, French interests now lie mainly in protecting the lucrative positions of a handful of corporations such as oil company Elf Acquitaine and construction giant Bouygues.
Foccart organised the first of many post-colonial military interventions to restore an ousted president in Gabon in 1964, setting a pattern that prevailed almost to the present day.
Chirac declared last year that the age of unilateral French intervention was over. But French troops have since been deployed twice in the Central African Republic to keep army mutineers at bay.

France still has some 8,200 troops permanently stationed in six African states. Government sources say the numbers will be reduced but no bases are likely to be closed under a reform of the armed forces ordered by Chirac.
When the president took office in May 1995, he rehabilitated the ailing Foccart, weakened by Parkinson's disease, taking him on his first African tour that year.

Side by side, an official Africa cell headed by former ambassador Michel Dupuch dispensed advice on good governance, while an unofficial unit of Foccart and his loyal collaborator Fernand Wibaux, a former espionage chief, maintained special relations with French-trained elites in place since the 1960s.
A historic "baron" in the Gaullist political family, Foccart had the president's ear. Chirac telephoned him almost daily for advice, Pean said.
